description: S2, option A: the same two orderings; member, reservation and copies locked, clock read after

results.required, collection commits first: collect=200 collected expire=false | reservation=COLLECTED copy=ON_LOAN (held by none) openLoans=1 activeItems=1 notices=0
results.required, expiry commits first: collect=409 not active expire=true | reservation=EXPIRED copy=AVAILABLE (held by none) openLoans=0 activeItems=0 notices=1

notes: Exactly one winner in every round, and every fact agrees with it.

The reservation is loaded for the first time under its lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in the SQL log) and the clock is read after the lock: the second transaction to arrive sees the first one's committed status, and the domain rule refuses it.

description: S2, option B: the same two orderings; a conditional UPDATE on the reservation decides

results.required, collection commits first: collect=200 collected expire=false | reservation=COLLECTED copy=ON_LOAN (held by none) openLoans=1 activeItems=1 notices=0
results.required, expiry commits first: collect=409 not active expire=true | reservation=EXPIRED copy=AVAILABLE (held by none) openLoans=0 activeItems=0 notices=1

notes: UPDATE reservation SET status=... WHERE id=? AND status='ACTIVE' AND expires_at > ?: 1 row, this transaction won; 0 rows, someone else decided first.
The second UPDATE waits for the first one's row lock, then PostgreSQL re-evaluates the WHERE on the committed row. The time rule now lives in Java and in the query.

description: S3, better: the late cancel reads only scalar keys before its locks
notes: Before the lock it reads a projection (reservation id, member id), not the entity: the persistence context stays empty, and the Reservation is loaded for the first time under the lock, with the committed COLLECTED status. 409, nothing changes.

description: S4, better: the late sweep releases only the copies Anna's reservation still holds
notes: Copy.releaseFrom(anna) answers false: the copy belongs to Bruno now. That is not an error, it is lazy expiry and the sweep agreeing.

description: S5, better: one lock order everywhere (member, reservation, copies) and a sweep that never waits
notes: No deadlock: the sweep asks for the member first, finds it locked by Anna's request (SKIP LOCKED) and skips the reservation at once. Anna never waits.
Skipping is safe: the old reservation stays ACTIVE and expired in the database, and the next run (expireAgain) expires it. The cost is bookkeeping a little later.

description: S6, better: two instances sweep the same 100 reservations, SKIP LOCKED
notes: For each reservation one worker takes the locks; the other skips it (row locked) or finds it already EXPIRED. Each reservation expires once, one notice each.

description: S6b, better: the same failure after the notice, with the notice sent after the commit
notes: The notice is published as an event and sent by a @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT): the rolled-back expiry sent nothing, and the reservation is still a candidate for the next run.
At most once: if the application died right after the commit, that notice would be lost. Exactly once needs an outbox table written in the same transaction.

description: S7, better: the same backlog of 1000, pages of 100, one transaction per reservation
notes: Each expiry commits on its own: its locks last milliseconds, so Bruno does not wait for the sweep, and the persistence context never holds more than one reservation's rows.
The failing reservation rolled back alone, sent nothing, and the next run expired it. With one run every 60 s, 1000 reservations take 10 runs: the interval is not a maximum delay.

description: S8, better: the same retried return; the loan row decides with a conditional update
notes: UPDATE loan SET returned=true WHERE id=? AND returned=false: 1 row for the first return, 0 for the retry, which then just answers with the returned loan.
Only the winner touches the copy, and only its status, and only if it is ON_LOAN: Bruno keeps his copy, and Clara is refused.

description: S7: a backlog of 1000 expired reservations, swept in one transaction
notes: Every expire() joined the sweep's transaction: all the reservations, copies and members stayed in one persistence context, and each auto-flush dirty-checked all of them.
A released copy stays locked until the final commit: Bruno waited for the whole sweep.
One failure rolled back every expiry, while the notices already sent stayed sent.
